planting.note: Establish from sprigs or plugs, not seed, since Coastcross-1 is a sterile hybrid; it was bred by Glenn Burton as an improvement on Coastal bermudagrass with markedly higher forage digestibility.

directions: Establish from sprigs or plugs in full sun into well-drained, fertile soil, since Coastcross-1 is a sterile hybrid and produces no viable seed. Bred by Glenn Burton as a refinement of his earlier Coastal release, Coastcross-1 was selected specifically for improved forage digestibility, resulting in better cattle weight gains per acre than Coastal despite similar overall yield, though it has less cold tolerance and is best suited to the milder parts of the Gulf South rather than more northerly bermudagrass range. It tolerates close, frequent grazing and rebounds vigorously with adequate moisture and fertility. Like other forage bermudagrass, it requires full sun and a consistent nitrogen fertility program to reach its full yield and quality potential.
sources: University of Georgia — Bermudagrass Forage Cultivar History
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars for Texas

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or plugs, not seed; Alicia is a taller, coarser-textured Texas-bred forage bermudagrass selected for high hay yield.

directions: Establish from sprigs or plugs in full sun into fertile, well-drained soil. Alicia is a tall-growing, coarse-textured Texas-bred forage bermudagrass developed for high hay yield rather than turf quality, producing more standing biomass per cutting than finer-textured turf-type bermudagrass cultivars. It responds strongly to nitrogen fertilization and consistent moisture, supporting multiple hay cuttings through the growing season. Its coarser leaf texture and taller growth habit make it unsuitable for lawns but well suited to hay production and pasture on Gulf South cattle operations. Like other bermudagrass, it needs full sun and declines rapidly under shade.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars for Texas
University of Georgia — Bermudagrass Forage Cultivar History

common_name: Russell Bermudagrass (High-Yield Forage and Hay Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or plugs, not seed; Russell is a popular Southern forage bermudagrass valued for its high hay yield and good cold tolerance for a hybrid bermudagrass.

directions: Establish from sprigs or plugs in full sun into fertile, well-drained soil. Russell is a widely planted forage bermudagrass cultivar in the South, prized for high hay and pasture yield combined with better cold tolerance than many hybrid bermudagrass types, allowing it to persist reliably across a broader range of the Gulf South and beyond. It responds well to a regular nitrogen fertility program and consistent moisture, supporting several hay cuttings per season, and tolerates close, frequent grazing when managed as pasture. As with all bermudagrass, full sun is essential, since even light shade quickly thins and weakens the stand.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars for Texas
University of Georgia — Bermudagrass Forage Cultivar History

common_name: Jiggs Bermudagrass (Cold-Hardy High-Yield Gulf Coast Forage Cultivar)

planting.note: Establish from sprigs, not seed; Jiggs is a Louisiana-origin forage bermudagrass that has become one of the most widely planted hay and pasture cultivars along the Gulf Coast for its cold tolerance and yield.

directions: Establish from fresh sprigs in full sun into fertile, well-drained soil, since Jiggs must be vegetatively propagated. Discovered in Louisiana and now one of the most extensively planted forage bermudagrass cultivars across the Gulf Coast, Jiggs is valued for a combination of high hay and pasture yield, good forage quality, and notably better cold tolerance than many other hybrid bermudagrasses, allowing it to hold stands through winters that damage less hardy cultivars. It establishes and spreads vigorously from sprigs and responds strongly to nitrogen fertility, supporting multiple hay cuttings through a long Gulf South growing season. Like all bermudagrass it requires full sun and thins quickly under shade.
